title: Momentum and the Gamblers Fallacy
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Written for Super Bowl Sunday, this piece takes on the statistical dismissal of momentum as a gambler's fallacy and presents research pushing back on that view. It first lays out the standard skeptical argument -- that past results have no bearing on future ones absent identical conditions -- then introduces data scientist Paul Roebber's analysis of ten years of NFL plays, which found that streaks of success across three or more series measurably raise a team's win probability, with winning teams showing 15 percent more of these momentum streaks than losing teams. The essay frames the practical leadership takeaway around harnessing self-reinforcing momentum once it appears, and recognizing how quickly it can shift.
points: Most statistical experts dismiss momentum as an instance of the gambler's fallacy -- believing past results predict future ones despite no causal link.
Data scientist Paul Roebber defines momentum as an increase in success sustained over three or more series (plays, at-bats, holes, etc.).
Analyzing ten years of NFL plays, Roebber found win probability rises substantially when a team accumulates momentum, especially late in games.
Winning teams in his dataset showed roughly 15 percent more momentum streaks than losing teams.
Because momentum is self-reinforcing, the best teams and leaders work to keep a streak of good outcomes alive once it starts, while staying aware of how fragile it is.
quotes: Momentum is real. If uninterrupted by the other team or competitors, this spirited force can take over a game and change the outcome in a flash.
Most statistical experts will tell you momentum isn't real and serves as just another example of the gambler's fallacy.
Roebber defines momentum as an increase in success over a span of three series.
After analyzing 10 years of every play in the NFL, Roebber found the chances of winning go way up when a team has more momentum, especially later in a game.
Teams that win have as much as 15 percent more of these momentum streaks than teams that lose.
They also know all too well that momentum is fragile and can shift back to the other team just as quickly.
